title: Zero to RHCSA on RHEL 10
description: Start with your first Linux login. Learn, troubleshoot and prove persistent administration skills on an AlmaLinux 10 client and server while preparing for the RHEL 10 RHCSA exam. Study in a browser or run the graded practicals in Erudior desktop.

modules.title: Your first Linux machine and shell
Shell scripts that other users can run

lessons.title: Meet Linux and install your first practice machine
lessons.body:
Your first support ticket says, “The reports are missing.” Before you can help, you need to know which computer holds the reports and how to ask it a question. A server is a computer providing something, such as files. A client is the computer requesting it. Either can run exactly the same operating system.

Linux supplies the kernel, which manages memory, devices and running programs. AlmaLinux 10 is the distribution you will run on both practice machines. Red Hat bases EX200 on Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 10. Each distribution packages that kernel with a shell, programs, documentation and an update service. A virtual machine (VM) runs a guest operating system on an emulated computer. The host is your everyday computer. Replacing a guest disk affects that guest, which is why we use disposable VMs here.

## Practice on AlmaLinux 10.3

[AlmaLinux 10.3 x86_64 DVD installer (10.82 GB)](https://repo.almalinux.org/almalinux/10.3/isos/x86_64/AlmaLinux-10.3-x86_64-dvd.iso) · [Practice kit ZIP](https://app.erudior.com/downloads/Erudior-AlmaLinux-10.3-Practice-Kit.zip)

The **Practice kit** sets up a private server and client. Open **Set up and reset the AlmaLinux 10.3 lab** in this lesson’s references for installation steps. The **Offline copy of the practice kit** reference also contains the complete ZIP. Choose the **rhcsa** profile for the shell, storage, services and networking exercises. For the machine-graded desktop exam, use the **Graded desktop template** section.

Once both guests pass their readiness checks, power them off and run `python3 lab.py capture rhcsa` on the host. Before each fresh practice attempt, run:

```bash
python3 lab.py reset rhcsa --start --offline
```

This returns both guests and their practice disks to the saved starting state. Copy out any evidence you want to keep before resetting.

## Build a first machine
If you already have the Erudior desktop lab image prepared, use **Start lab** in the practice-console lesson and return here when you see a guest login. Otherwise use your virtualization program’s **New virtual machine** action. Get the AlmaLinux OS 10 DVD ISO for your guest architecture from AlmaLinux. Choose the standard x86_64 build for the Erudior desktop pair and compare the image’s SHA-256 digest to the matching entry on AlmaLinux’s download page. An ISO acts like an installation disc. For this course a practical starting size for each manually installed guest is 2 virtual CPUs, 4 GiB RAM and a new 30 GiB virtual disk. Use a private or NAT network. Keep the host's physical disks detached.

Boot the guest from the ISO. Choose your language, time zone and installation destination. Check the capacity against your new virtual disk. Select automatic partitioning and a minimal or server software environment. Create a user named `learner`, give it a password you know and select the administrator option. Complete installation, eject the virtual DVD and restart. Log in at the console. In a graphical session open **Terminal**. Password entry on a text console gives no visual feedback. Type the password and press Enter.

## Your first receipt
Run `whoami`, then `cat /etc/os-release`. Expect your username, `ID="almalinux"` (quotes may be omitted), and a VERSION_ID starting with 10. Read these values inside each guest. Run `hostnamectl` and identify the operating system and the hostname as two different pieces of information. If you installed this VM yourself, shut down from inside the guest with `sudo systemctl poweroff`. Take a powered-off snapshot named **clean-install**, start the VM and confirm you can log in again. For Erudior’s managed machines, use **Stop lab** and reopen the same lesson to resume your disks. If your self-installed VM shows the installer again, change the virtual boot order or eject the ISO.

**Try it independently.** Point to the host, guest, guest console and virtual disk in your setup. Explain which one would lose the files if you restored the snapshot. Browser-only learners can follow the observations and quizzes immediately. To build operational skill, perform the exercises in your own guests or use the desktop consoles when available.

[AlmaLinux downloads and checksums](https://almalinux.org/get-almalinux/) · [RHEL 10 installation and administration documentation](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10)

lessons.title: Read a prompt and recover from a typing mistake
lessons.body:
A terminal carries keystrokes and output. A shell reads a line, splits it into words and starts a command. In a prompt such as `[learner@client ~]$`, learner is the account, client is the hostname, and the tilde stands for that user's home directory. The dollar sign is the prompt. Type the text that follows it in examples.

Start as your ordinary user. Type `pwd` and press Enter. It prints your working directory, often `/home/learner`. Type `ls -ld /etc`. The first word chooses the program. The option `-d` asks for the directory itself, and `-l` asks for its long listing. The last word is the object to inspect. Compare it with `ls /etc`, which lists the directory's children. You can read a system directory without having permission to change it.

## Learn to get unstuck
Type `printf '%s\n' 'night shift'`. The quotes group the two words into one argument. Use the Up arrow to recall that command and edit the text. Now type an opening single quote without a closing quote and press Enter. Bash gives a continuation prompt because the command is incomplete. Press Ctrl+C to cancel it. Run `sleep 30` and use Ctrl+C again to return to the prompt. For a long listing piped to `less`, press q to leave the pager.

**Read the evidence.** Run `ls /no-such-training-path` and then `echo $?`. A diagnostic names the missing path and the status is nonzero. Run `pwd` and immediately inspect the status again. Zero records success for that command. Each new command replaces the previous status.

**Try it independently.** Without retyping the successful listing, recall it and inspect /var. Show how you would tell the difference between a shell waiting for the rest of a quotation, a pager awaiting a key, and a command that has already failed and returned to the prompt.

lessons.title: Choose your workspace and identify both machines
lessons.body:
You are the on-call administrator for a small office. The server supplies files and services. The client represents the workstation whose users need them. By the final practical you will make changes on both machines, verify them from the affected user's point of view, and leave them working after startup.

## Before you begin
Start with the installation and first-prompt lessons if you are new to Linux. In a browser, read the same lessons and take their quizzes here. For hands-on work, open the **Build your own client and server** reference below and use the two guest terminals beside the course. Browser readers without guests can use the observation exercises first and revisit the work orders when they have a pair.

## Erudior desktop workspace

The desktop app runs a client and server on your computer. Windows uses Debian under WSL 2, macOS uses a local Lima instance named `erudior-labs`, and Linux uses QEMU directly. Open **First-time setup** in a VM lesson for your platform's instructions. Inside the Linux provider, install QEMU 9.2 or newer and a prepared, BIOS-bootable x86-64 AlmaLinux 10 cloud image. The host supplies both guests from the same image. Reserve 3 GiB for the two guests, plus memory for the provider and the desktop.

Start with the official AlmaLinux 10 x86_64 Generic Cloud qcow2. Match its SHA-256 against the value published for that exact build. Prepare a separate copy with the guest tools in **Build your own client and server** while it has package access. Windows and macOS use Debian to host QEMU. The systems at the two guest consoles run AlmaLinux. The engine supplies cloud-init configuration and a learner account. While preparing the template, install the tools in the **Prepare the services used by the work orders** section of the manual-pair reference on both machines as appropriate. For the shared desktop base, install the union of both package lists. The desktop setup guide gives the full list and the cloud-init cleanup step. Place it inside the provider at `~/.local/share/erudior-vm-labs/images/almalinux-10-rhcsa.qcow2` for the default data directory.

## Make a baseline
In Erudior desktop, open **Practice consoles and an on-demand mount**, select **Start lab** and wait for both guests. Stop at login for now. If you built your own pair, open their consoles. Open each console in turn. In Erudior desktop, **Console login** gives this attempt's credentials for `learner`. On your own VM, use the account you created. Run the following in each guest.

```sh
hostname
cat /etc/redhat-release
id
ip -brief address
cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id
```

On both consoles run `cat /etc/os-release`. Record ID, VERSION_ID and hostname together. Expect almalinux and a 10.x release on both. Write down which guest owns `192.168.77.10` and which owns `192.168.77.20`. Hostname, address and boot ID together identify where and when you observed an outcome. If the prompt is silent during first boot, let cloud-init finish and press Enter. Use `sudo` for changes inside these guests. If the learner or guest address differs, confirm you opened a console from this lesson.

## How to study
Use the untimed pair for the worked examples. Return to the same lesson to resume it. A graded lesson opens its own fresh pair on the first attempt. **Prepare machines** boots the pair and **Begin** starts the deadline. In a timed attempt, leaving the lesson keeps the clock running. When switching lessons, stop the untimed workspace with **Stop lab**, or stop a completed practical after its result is saved. This keeps just two guests running on the host. Stopping the pair preserves its disks. **Reset disks** discards that lesson's guest changes. The final samples ten tasks. Do the self-checks as well to practice the wider EX200 objectives.

lessons.title: Practice consoles and an on-demand mount
lessons.body:
**First visit.** Open a terminal on each guest and identify it with `hostname` and `id`. Continue to the shell lessons. Return to the mount exercise below when you reach network filesystems. If you use your own VMs, prepare the export using **Build your own client and server**.

This is your reusable workshop. You can open both consoles here while following later lessons. **Check my work** in this workspace grades only the on-demand network mount. You can return after the file systems module and repeat the check.

## Trace a request between the guests
On the server, run `sudo exportfs -v` and `cat /srv/projects/erudior-lab.txt`. Note the allowed client and the first few characters of the file. On the client, run `ip route get 192.168.77.10`. Look for the outgoing interface and source address. Confirm both guests' addresses before editing.

## Make one mount work
On the client, create `/etc/auto.master.d/workshop.autofs` containing the first line below. Create `/etc/auto.workshop` containing the second line. Each file has one line. A direct map uses a full client path as its key.

```text
/- /etc/auto.workshop
/mnt/projects -fstype=nfs,ro 192.168.77.10:/srv/projects
```

Run `sudo systemctl enable --now autofs` and `sudo systemctl reload autofs`. Then run `cat /mnt/projects/erudior-lab.txt` and `findmnt -T /mnt/projects/erudior-lab.txt` on the client. Expect the same marker as on the server and an NFS filesystem. A missing path calls for checking the master file's `.autofs` suffix, the map key and the service journal.

Choose **Check my work** when ready. It reboots the client and checks again. Read the before/after observations. Reopen this lesson for future walkthroughs and keep your own evidence in a notebook. In later graded labs, keep working until you have checked the requested state, then choose **Submit exam**.

lessons.title: Find your way through a Linux filesystem
lessons.body:
A pathname describes a walk through directories. An absolute path starts at the root directory, written /. A relative path starts at the process's current directory. Each shell has its own working directory. A colleague's instruction to “edit reports/today” is ambiguous until you know where they started.

## Make a work area
Open a regular-user terminal. Work in a fresh directory. Use `mkdir -p ~/shift-practice/inbox ~/shift-practice/archive` and `cd ~/shift-practice`. The shell expands ~ to your home directory. Run `pwd` and `ls -a`. A single dot refers to this directory and two dots to its parent. Create an empty file with `touch 'inbox/shift notes'`, then try `ls -l 'inbox/shift notes'`. Move into inbox and ask Bash for the same path again. From here that relative path asks for an inbox *inside* inbox. Use `ls -l 'shift notes'` to identify the same file.

## Give the next shift a copy
From inbox run `cp 'shift notes' ../archive/day-one`. Rename the original with `mv 'shift notes' 'shift report'`. List both directories. A copy has its own content and name. Renaming the source leaves the copy's name alone. Use `ls -ld /etc /var /home /run`. Configuration commonly lives in /etc, changing service data in /var, personal work in /home and runtime state in /run. Remember where to look when a setting disappears on restart.

**Independent ticket.** Starting in your home directory, put a second copy of day-one in inbox under the name day-two. Remove only day-two with `rm -i` and confirm what still exists with `find ~/shift-practice -type f`. Your two original files should remain. If a pathname contains spaces, quote the whole pathname or use Tab completion. A missing-file error gives you a pathname to check before changing privileges.

lessons.title: Edit a configuration and find help offline
lessons.body:
Many system settings are text files. An editor changes the file on disk. A service may keep using its previously loaded settings until you reload it. First practice where a typo affects only your home directory.

Run `mkdir -p ~/editor-practice` and `cd ~/editor-practice`. Create a known starting point with `printf 'owner=morning\nqueue=1\n' > shift.conf`. Make a backup with `cp -p shift.conf shift.conf.before`. Open `vi shift.conf`. In normal mode type `/morning` and press Enter to find the word. Press `cw`, type `evening`, press Esc and type `:wq` followed by Enter. If you get lost before saving, Esc then `:q!` discards that edit. Compare files with `diff -u shift.conf.before shift.conf`. Lines with minus and plus show the old and new values. An exit status of one from diff means the files differ.

For a command whose options you have forgotten, ask the installed manual. Open `man cp`, search for `/preserve`, use n for the next match and q to quit. Compare `man 1 passwd` (the program) with `man 5 passwd` (the account record format). Use `info coreutils` where installed. Locate package documents with `rpm -qd coreutils` and inspect `/usr/share/doc`. A minimal image may need man-db, man-pages, info or package documentation installed from its configured source.

**Independent ticket.** Add a third line, `region=west`, without changing the first two. Show the exact change in a diff, then restore the original from your backup. Run `cmp shift.conf.before shift.conf` and inspect its status. A silent successful comparison is a useful receipt.

lessons.title: Follow data through a pipeline
lessons.body:
A program can read standard input and write to two places: its ordinary output and its diagnostic output. A pipe carries the first program's standard output into the next program's standard input. This lets one person write a filter and another decide where its results should go.

In a fresh directory under your home, create a small shift log.

```sh
printf '%s\n' '08:00 OK bay-1' '08:10 ERROR bay-2' '08:20 OK bay-2' '08:30 ERROR bay-3' > shift.log
grep ' ERROR ' shift.log
grep ' ERROR ' shift.log | wc -l
```

The first pipeline stage selects whole lines. The second counts newline characters, so expect two. Try `grep '^08:10' shift.log`. The caret anchors the match at the beginning. Compare `grep -E 'bay-[23]$' shift.log` with `grep -F 'bay-[23]$' shift.log`. The first interprets the character class and end anchor. The second looks for those literal characters. Keep shell quotes around a pattern so the shell passes it to grep unchanged.

## Decide what to keep
Run `grep ' ERROR ' shift.log > alerts` twice. The second run replaces the old output. Add one line using `printf '%s\n' 'manually reviewed' >> alerts`; the double angle brackets append. Now run `cat shift.log missing-file > collected 2> diagnostics`. Read both new files. The valid lines survived even though one input failed. A nonempty output file by itself cannot certify a successful run.

**Independent ticket.** Produce a file containing just the bay-2 events, in time order, and a separate count. Predict both lines before checking. Search for a bay you know is absent and immediately inspect grep's exit status. Status 1 means no match; a missing input file typically gives status 2. Decide whether each deserves the same alert.

lessons.title: Predict who can read, change or enter a path
lessons.body:
Linux checks the caller's identity against the file's owner, group and other permission classes. Read the first character of `ls -l` for the file type, then the three permission triplets. For a regular file, r reads data, w changes data and x permits execution. For a directory, r lists names, x traverses to a known entry, and w with x allows changes to directory entries. Deleting a file is a change to its parent directory.

Run the following as your ordinary user in an empty directory you own. The parentheses start a subshell so the changed umask lasts only for this exercise.

```sh
(umask 027; mkdir crew; touch crew/notes; stat -c '%a %n' crew crew/notes)
chmod u=rw,g=r,o= crew/notes
ls -ld crew crew/notes
```

A new ordinary file commonly starts from requested mode 666, a directory from 777. A mask of 027 removes group write and all permissions for others. Expect 640 for notes and 750 for crew. A mask removes bits from what was requested, so it cannot grant execute permission to a new ordinary file. Existing objects keep their earlier mode.

**Diagnose one failure.** Temporarily remove your own search permission with `chmod u-x crew`. Predict whether `cat crew/notes` works. Run it, then `namei -l "$PWD/crew/notes"` to inspect every path component. Restore traversal with `chmod u+x crew`. Confirm the file is still 640. An administrator testing as root can miss this denial.

**Independent ticket.** Give the owner read/write, group read, and others no access on a second file using numeric mode. Set the parent directory so its group can enter and list it. Explain why group members who can list the filename might still fail to open the file.

lessons.title: Find evidence and build a shared directory
lessons.body:
A colleague reports that overnight copies failed. Work as learner on the untimed client. Choose an unused directory name for this run. Make a private practice directory and turn a noisy log into an archive someone else can inspect.

```sh
install -d -m 700 ~/rhcsa-tools && cd ~/rhcsa-tools
printf '%s\n' 'OK copied' 'ERR read' 'OK copied' 'ERR write' > run.log
grep '^ERR ' run.log | sort > errors.txt
wc -l < errors.txt
ln run.log run.hard
ln -s run.log run.link
ls -li run*
tar -czf evidence.tar.gz run.log errors.txt
tar -tzf evidence.tar.gz
```

Expect two errors, the same inode for the two hard-linked names, and a symbolic link containing a pathname. Rename `run.log` to `night.log`. Predict which link still reads the log, then test each. Capture the failed read with `cat run.link 2>link-error.txt`. Restore the name and verify the symbolic link works again. Create a bzip2 version with `tar -cjf evidence.tar.bz2 run.log` after restoring the name. Run `mkdir from-gzip from-bzip2`. Extract the archives with `tar -xzf evidence.tar.gz -C from-gzip` and `tar -xjf evidence.tar.bz2 -C from-bzip2`. Check both restored copies with `cmp run.log from-gzip/run.log` and `cmp run.log from-bzip2/run.log`. Both should exit zero. Look up flags using `man tar`, `info coreutils` or `/usr/share/doc`.

## A directory shared by a team
On the server, create a practice group with `sudo groupadd editors` if absent. Run `sudo install -d -g editors -m 2770 /srv/editorial`. With `stat -c '%A %a %G' /srv/editorial` expect `drwxrws--- 2770 editors`. Directory execute permission allows traversal. Setgid makes newly created children inherit the directory's group. It does not grant write permission by itself.

Try it with `sudo touch /srv/editorial/draft` and inspect the group on the child. If a user cannot enter a path despite suitable final permissions, inspect every ancestor with `namei -l /srv/editorial/draft`. In a clean practice directory, try `cp`, `mv`, a text editor, and `rm -i` on your own disposable file to practice the file lifecycle.

## Search text and redirect streams
Regular expressions select lines by pattern. `grep -E '^(ERR|WARN) ' run.log` matches lines that start with either word. In basic syntax without `-E`, `|` and parentheses are literal characters unless escaped. Add `-v` to invert the match, `-c` to count matching lines, `-i` to ignore case and `-n` to show line numbers. Anchors `^` and `$` mark the start and end of a line.

`>` replaces a file and `>>` appends. `2>` sends standard error elsewhere. Redirections apply left to right, so `command >> all.log 2>&1` appends both streams, while `command 2>&1 >> all.log` still sends errors to the terminal. A pipe `|` connects standard output only.

To act as another user in a full login environment run `su - USER`, or `sudo -i -u USER` where sudo policy allows it. `su` without `-` keeps much of your current environment, including the working directory. Leave the other user's shell with `exit`.

lessons.title: Lab • Hand off a team workspace
lessons.body:
On the **server**, prepare `/srv/team` for `labops`. This group is local to the server. Create it here if needed. Team members need full directory access, others need none, and new entries should inherit the team group. The requested final mode is `2770`.

Before submission, inspect the directory itself, create a disposable child inside it, and check the child's group. Remove your test child. If the mode reads `0770`, identify which special bit is missing. If the group is wrong only on a child created earlier, repeat with a new file. Submit when the directory is correct and review the post-reboot result.

## Reason through a reported result
A teammate can enter /srv/team, but a newly created note belongs to the writer’s primary group. The directory listing reads drwxrwx---. Which observation explains this?

**Check your reasoning.** Group write and search work, but the directory lacks the setgid bit. Inspect the directory itself, then create a new child after repair. Existing files keep their previous group.

lessons.title: Understand a login, a group and a privileged command
lessons.body:
A login name is the human label for a numeric user ID. Permissions use the numeric identity. A process also carries a primary group and may carry extra groups. Two machines may have the same login name and different users behind it. Start on the client and run `whoami`, `id` and `getent passwd "$(id -un)"`. Read the account name, numeric IDs, home directory and login shell from the colon-separated account record. The x in the password field tells you that password verification data is stored separately.

Run `sudo -l` and read which commands your account may request. Use `sudo id -u` if allowed. It prints 0 when that single command runs as root. Follow it with `id -u` to see your original shell identity. To test another account's view on your own VM, start a new login shell with `sudo -iu learner` from an authorized administrator account. Compare `pwd`, `id` and `printf '%s\n' "$HOME"`, then `exit` to return. A new shell is a separate process and inherits a set of credentials at startup.

**Worked diagnosis.** You add a person to an existing group. The account database immediately lists both groups when you run `id USERNAME`. In their open terminal, plain `id` still shows the earlier list. Ask them to start a fresh login and repeat both checks. Changing ownership on every team file would address a different problem.

**Independent ticket.** On the client, find learner's login shell and primary group. In a fresh learner session, identify the effective user for a privileged read-only command. Record which machine answered. Explain why that result tells you nothing about who may run the same command on the server.

lessons.title: Onboard an operator without losing existing access
lessons.body:
An operator should join a second team without losing an earlier assignment. On the untimed client, use spare names for this exercise. Check `getent passwd fieldops`, `getent group dispatch`, `getent group editors-local` and `getent group editors-night` first. On a fresh guest the names should be unused.

```sh
sudo groupadd dispatch
sudo groupadd editors-local
sudo useradd -m -G dispatch fieldops
sudo usermod -aG editors-local fieldops
id fieldops
sudo chage -M 90 -W 7 fieldops
sudo chage -l fieldops
sudo -iu fieldops id
```

Expect both supplementary groups and a 90-day maximum age. `usermod -G` replaces the supplementary list unless you append. Existing shells keep their group credentials until a new login. Set a password interactively with `sudo passwd fieldops` and verify the aging policy again. Avoid putting passwords in shell history. Rename a group with `groupmod -n NEW OLD`, lock an account with `usermod -L` and unlock it with `usermod -U`. Change a primary group with `usermod -g`; that does not touch supplementary groups.

## Rename a group and verify its identity

Record the numeric GID from `getent group editors-local`. Run `sudo groupmod -n editors-night editors-local` and compare `getent group editors-night`, `getent group editors-local` and `id fieldops`. Expect the same GID and the same membership under the new name. The old name should no longer resolve. What happens to a file owned by this GID?

## Delegate one administrative action
Locate `systemctl` with `command -v systemctl`. Use `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/fieldops-status` to grant the exact command (adjust its path if necessary).

```text
fieldops ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl is-active chronyd.service
```

Run `sudo visudo -c` and `sudo -l -U fieldops`. Compare the granted command and arguments to the request. To retire only this practice identity, remove the new sudoers entry, run `sudo userdel -r fieldops`, then check that the practice groups are empty and run `sudo groupdel editors-night` and `sudo groupdel dispatch`. Verify the lookups now return no record. A local account or group on the client has a separate database from one with the same name on the server.

lessons.title: Lab • Add a client operator
lessons.body:
On the **client**, create the local account `labtech` and give it membership in `labops`. Preserve any other membership the account has. The group on the server belongs to the other guest and cannot grant access here. Create a local `labops` group on the client if `getent group labops` finds none.

Check `getent passwd labtech`, `getent group labops` and `id labtech`. A blank member list in a group record can still be consistent with a primary group, so judge effective membership with `id`. Switch to a fresh login context to see the groups a new process would receive. Submit and compare the membership checks across the reboot.

## Reason through a reported result
A fresh client login lists labops, while an older labtech shell still lists its previous groups. Which result should you trust for the next login?

**Check your reasoning.** The fresh login has the new process credentials. Check the account database as well. Existing shells keep their previous supplementary groups.

lessons.title: Follow one connection from client to service
lessons.body:
Imagine that a browser on the client asks the server for a report. It needs an address for the server, a route to that address, a listening service at a port, and permission for the traffic to reach it. Each question has a different observer. Start at the client for name and route. Inspect the server for a listener and its firewall.

An IPv4 address such as 192.168.77.20 identifies an interface on this network. The /24 prefix describes its network portion. The client can ordinarily reach 192.168.77.10 directly on the same private network. To reach a different network, it usually sends to a gateway. An IPv6 example, 2001:db8:42::20/64, uses the same address-and-prefix idea with more bits. A port identifies an application endpoint on an address. Resolving a name proves only that an address was returned.

## Draw your two machines
On each guest run `hostname` and `ip -br address`. Label the interfaces, addresses and prefixes in a two-row table. The lo interface and 127.0.0.1 or ::1 point back to the current guest. Ask the client which path it would use with `ip route get 192.168.77.10`. Read the device and source address. An answer to this command is the kernel's route choice; it does not send a request to the server.

On the server run `ss -lnt`. If SSH is running, look for TCP port 22 and read the address to its left. A service bound only to 127.0.0.1 accepts local connections. A listener bound to 0.0.0.0 accepts connections addressed to any local IPv4 interface, subject to firewall and service policy.

**Independent ticket.** The file server resolves to 127.0.0.1 on the client. The server shows a healthy listener. Explain which machine the client actually contacted. Use `getent hosts` with the reported name, compare both address inventories, and describe the smallest correction. In the next lesson you will persist a hostname mapping and a separate dual-stack interface profile.

lessons.title: Trace a request from name to interface to listener
lessons.body:
A user can reach a file server by address but cannot reach it by name. Test the same name lookup the application uses before changing routes. On the client compare `getent ahostsv4 server.workshop.test`, `ip route get 192.168.77.10` and `ip -brief address`. On the server inspect listening TCP sockets with `ss -lnt`. A resolver failure, missing route and closed listener have different remedies.

Add `192.168.77.10 server.workshop.test` once to the client's `/etc/hosts`, then run `getent ahostsv4 server.workshop.test | awk '{print $1}' | sort -u`. Expect one unique address. Multiple rows for stream and datagram socket types are normal. Check `grep '^hosts:' /etc/nsswitch.conf` to see where applications look up hosts. `dig` queries DNS directly and may miss a valid local hosts entry.

## Configure a practice interface without changing the lab link
In the untimed client with NetworkManager available, create a dummy profile. Check that `workshop-dummy` and `dummy42` are unused first.

```sh
sudo nmcli connection add type dummy ifname dummy42 con-name workshop-dummy ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.0.2.44/24 ipv6.method manual ipv6.addresses 2001:db8:42::44/64
sudo nmcli connection modify workshop-dummy connection.autoconnect yes
sudo nmcli connection up workshop-dummy
ip -brief address show dummy42
nmcli -f connection.autoconnect,ipv4.addresses,ipv6.addresses connection show workshop-dummy
```

Verify both addresses and the autoconnect setting. Reboot the workshop guest and verify again. Remove only the practice profile using `sudo nmcli connection delete workshop-dummy`. Keep the engine-provided interface unchanged. A connection profile persists configuration; commands such as `ip addr add` change runtime state.

## Change an existing profile and the hostname
Tasks usually modify the profile that already exists for an interface. Find it with `nmcli connection show` and `nmcli device status`. Practice on the dummy profile before you remove it:

```sh
sudo nmcli connection modify workshop-dummy ipv4.gateway 192.0.2.1 ipv4.dns 192.0.2.53 ipv4.dns-search workshop.test
sudo nmcli connection modify workshop-dummy +ipv6.addresses 2001:db8:42::45/64
sudo nmcli connection up workshop-dummy
nmcli -f ipv4,ipv6 connection show workshop-dummy | grep -E 'addresses|gateway|dns'
```

`+` adds to a list property instead of replacing it. A change to a profile takes effect when the connection is activated again. Profiles are stored as keyfiles under `/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections`; `nmtui` edits the same profiles interactively. NetworkManager writes `/etc/resolv.conf` from active profiles, so DNS servers belong in the profile rather than a hand edit of that file.

Set a persistent static hostname with `sudo hostnamectl set-hostname NAME` and check it with `hostnamectl` and a new login. The `hostname` command alone changes only the running system. Restore the guest's original hostname when you finish, because the course uses it to tell the guests apart.

lessons.title: Lab • Make the file server discoverable
lessons.body:
On the **client**, make `files.lab.test` consistently resolve to the server at `192.168.77.10` for IPv4 applications, including after startup. Preserve the existing localhost and guest mappings.

Look up the exact name with `getent ahostsv4` and list its distinct addresses. A ping to the numeric IP only tests a different part of the path. If two different addresses appear, inspect the matching hosts entries and the resolver order. Recheck with a fresh command before submitting.

## Reason through a reported result
A direct-address SSH connection works, but getent ahostsv4 files.lab.test returns nothing. Which layer will you change?

**Check your reasoning.** IP connectivity is already demonstrated. Check the client’s name-service order and its persistent mapping for the exact hostname, then repeat the application lookup.

lessons.title: Follow software from a trusted source to an installed file
lessons.body:
A user asks for the program that inspects a directory tree. Your system can answer three different questions. The shell can locate an executable on its search path. The RPM database can tell you which installed package owns a file. DNF can query available repositories to find software even before installation. A successful repository listing alone installs nothing.

Run `command -v bash`, `rpm -q bash` and `rpm -ql bash | head`. Write one sentence for each result. Compare `rpm -q tree` with `dnf info tree` on an AlmaLinux guest with BaseOS and AppStream enabled. DNF might show a candidate version while RPM reports no installed package. If DNF cannot find metadata, inspect `dnf repolist --enabled`, the source URL and whether that AlmaLinux guest can reach its mirror or has matching installation media attached.

## Observe a transaction
On your disposable guest with a working source, select a small optional package that is not already installed, such as tree. Run `sudo dnf install tree`. Read the transaction summary before accepting. Check `rpm -q tree`, run `tree --version`, and ask `rpm -qf "$(command -v tree)"` which package supplied it. Try `dnf check-update tree`; status 100 means updates are available. When a newer build exists, apply `sudo dnf upgrade tree` and compare versions. Use `sudo dnf remove tree` to retire your practice installation and inspect the removal summary before confirming. Restore the previous state if you started with a different package.

AlmaLinux uses distribution mirrors. Red Hat’s CDN serves signed RHEL packages to a registered, entitled RHEL machine. Practice the RHEL-specific registration steps in the manual-pair reference if you have access to RHEL. An internal RPM repository can use an approved HTTPS URL. The repository root must contain its repodata directory. A local RPM file also needs trusted signing keys and available dependencies. A Flatpak remote distributes applications and runtimes separately from the host RPM database. User-scope commands act for the account that runs them.

**Independent ticket.** One learner can launch a Flatpak application and a second account cannot find it. Predict what `flatpak list --user --app` in each login and `flatpak list --system --app` will show. Explain how you would select the intended scope before installing a second copy. Use the next workshop to add the remote and prove installation and removal.

lessons.title: Choose and verify a software source
lessons.body:
A branch office receives software over removable media. DNF needs a repository root containing `repodata/repomd.xml`. The URL refers to that root. A repository ID identifies the entry to DNF, while `name` is a human-readable label.

## Inspect a local repository
The client includes an empty practice repository. In the untimed client create `/etc/yum.repos.d/workshop.repo` with this content, then validate only that source.

```ini
[workshop]
name=Workshop shelf
baseurl=file:///srv/erudior-repo
enabled=1
gpgcheck=1
```

```sh
test -r /srv/erudior-repo/repodata/repomd.xml
dnf repolist --enabled
sudo dnf --disablerepo='*' --enablerepo=workshop makecache
rpm -q bash
rpm -qf /usr/bin/bash
```

Metadata refresh should succeed even though the shelf has no application packages. For a local RPM, obtain the expected signing key and its fingerprint from the trusted publisher. On a guest with the verified key in its RPM keyring run `rpmkeys --checksig --verbose ./package.rpm` on the actual file. Look for an OK signature from the expected key. Digests alone establish file integrity. Install with `sudo dnf --setopt=localpkg_gpgcheck=1 install ./package.rpm` to enforce local-file signature checks. Trusted repositories must supply any dependencies. Use `rpm -q NAME` to verify the installed version. On AlmaLinux, query the enabled sources with `dnf repolist` and update a practice package with `sudo dnf upgrade NAME` when a newer build exists. Review the transaction before removing a package you added with `sudo dnf remove NAME`.

For a network repository, obtain an approved HTTPS repository root and its key file. Create a separate [workshop-net] section with this baseurl, enabled=1, gpgcheck=1 and gpgkey pointing to the approved key. Test `sudo dnf --disablerepo='*' --enablerepo=workshop-net makecache` and query a package available in that source.

## Self-check with a Flatpak remote
Use a guest with Flatpak and a reachable approved .flatpakrepo descriptor. Record `flatpak remotes --user --show-details` and `flatpak list --user --app`. Choose an unused remote name (training below) and an app absent from this account. Run `flatpak remote-add --user training /path/to/training.flatpakrepo` with the actual descriptor. Confirm the new URL from remote details. Run `flatpak remote-ls --user --app training`, choose a listed app and run `flatpak install --user training APP_ID`. Confirm its exact ID using `flatpak list --user --app`. Remove that ID with `flatpak uninstall --user APP_ID` and check the list again. Remove only newly installed practice refs before running `flatpak remote-delete --user training`. Keep existing apps, runtimes and remotes.

On an Internet-connected disposable guest where Flathub is approved, the remote-add step can use `flatpak remote-add --user training https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo`. A disconnected guest needs a supplied remote with accessible app and runtime content.

Without `--user`, `flatpak remote-add` and `flatpak install` act on the system-wide installation and need administrative rights. Read the task for which scope it wants, then verify with `flatpak remotes` and `flatpak list --app` (system) or the same commands with `--user`.

lessons.title: Lab • Bring an offline RPM source online
lessons.body:
On the **client**, enable one DNF repository with the repository ID `erudior-local` (the section name in brackets) using only `file:///srv/erudior-repo` as its base URL and require RPM signature checks. The files under that directory are supplied. Complete the task with the prepared local content.

Verify that the enabled repository list shows the ID, that a metadata refresh restricted to that ID succeeds, and that its configuration sets `gpgcheck=1`. Watch for an extra `repodata` component, a duplicate section ID in another file, or a stale `mirrorlist` or `metalink`. The supplied shelf is empty, so an empty list of available packages can accompany a working configuration.

## Reason through a reported result
The shelf appears in repolist; makecache for that source alone reports that repomd.xml cannot be found. What has each test established?

**Check your reasoning.** DNF parsed an enabled entry. The second test actually tried its URL. Inspect the base directory and its repodata/repomd.xml, then refresh just that source again.

lessons.title: Tell a process, a shell job and a service apart
lessons.body:
When you launch a command, the kernel gives its process a numeric ID (PID). A shell can keep track of jobs it started. A service manager can start and supervise processes even after an administrator logs out. These are three views of running work. Killing a process belonging to a service can trigger its restart policy.

## Watch one harmless process
Start `sleep 120 &` as your regular user. The ampersand returns control of the terminal immediately. Save its PID with `worker=$!`, then run `jobs -l` and `ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,ni,comm -p "$worker"`. The parent PID identifies the process that launched it. A sleeping process usually consumes almost no CPU. Use `top`, press P to sort by CPU or M for memory, then q to exit. Compare a process's resident memory with the system view in `free -h`. Linux uses spare memory as cache; the available column includes memory it can make available to programs.

Open another terminal as the same user. Its `jobs` list does not show the first shell's job, while `ps -p PID` with the recorded number can still see it. Back in the original shell, check the PID still identifies your sleep process, then run `kill -TERM "$worker"`. Use `wait "$worker"` followed by `ps -p "$worker"` to observe completion. TERM requests termination and allows a program to clean up. Select a specific disposable process for this exercise.

**Independent ticket.** A dashboard lists two processes with the same name. Show how to distinguish them using PID, owner and parent. Before adjusting priority, decide whether the symptom is CPU contention or a process waiting for I/O. In the next exercise, predict the direction of a nice-value change before you apply it.

lessons.title: Follow a slowdown from process to journal
lessons.body:
A server is sluggish after a scheduled job. Start with evidence from the current boot. On the workshop server, run `uptime`, `free -h` and `ps -eo pid,user,ni,pcpu,pmem,comm --sort=-pcpu | head`. Reorder by `-pmem` to find memory consumers. Load, CPU use and memory pressure answer different questions. `top` shows the same ranking live; press `P` or `M` to sort, `k` to signal a process and `q` to quit. `pkill -u USER NAME` and `kill PID` send TERM by default. Use `kill -KILL` only after TERM has had a chance, because the process cannot clean up.

## Follow one process you own
```sh
nice -n 5 sleep 300 &
jobpid=$!
ps -o pid,ni,stat,comm -p "$jobpid"
renice -n 10 -p "$jobpid"
ps -o pid,ni,stat,comm -p "$jobpid"
kill -TERM "$jobpid"
wait "$jobpid"
```

Use a shell starting at nice value 0. The initial +5 is relative to the shell. If ps races the launch, repeat it once sleep appears. Expect nice 5, then 10 after renice. Bash wait normally returns 143 when TERM ends the sleep. A higher nice number gives a normal process a lower scheduling priority. Diagnose a service with `systemctl status NAME` and `journalctl -b -u NAME`, replacing NAME with the unit. Record the first failure and its timestamp. To preserve messages on a default journald setup using `Storage=auto`, create `/var/log/journal` with sudo, run `sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create --prefix /var/log/journal` then `sudo journalctl --flush`. If policy explicitly sets volatile storage, configure `Storage=persistent` in a journald drop-in and restart journald. Write `logger -t workshop-boot 'workshop boot evidence'`. After a planned workshop reboot check `sudo journalctl -b -1 -t workshop-boot` or search the previous boot by message.

## Choose a tuning profile
Run `tuned-adm list`, `tuned-adm recommend` and `tuned-adm active`. Record the current profile name before changing it. On the workshop server choose an installed profile such as `balanced` with `sudo tuned-adm profile balanced`. Verify with `tuned-adm active` and `sudo tuned-adm verify`. Explain why maximizing throughput and reducing energy use can favor different settings. Restore the prior profile when finished.

lessons.title: Read a failure in the journal and preserve its evidence
lessons.body:
The first useful error often appears several lines before a final “failed” status. The journal records the unit, boot, timestamp and message. Choose the scope before drawing a conclusion. If a request failed after a reboot, the current boot may be healthy while yesterday's evidence has gone.

On your disposable system, choose a new unique name, for example `unit=shift-check-$(date +%s)`. Use `sudo systemd-run --unit="$unit" /usr/bin/false`. This asks systemd to run a temporary service whose program deliberately exits with status 1. The launcher may report that it scheduled the unit successfully. Run `sudo systemctl status "$unit.service" --no-pager` and `sudo journalctl -b -u "$unit.service" --no-pager`. Identify the executable, the exit status and the subsequent unit failure. The launch request and the program's outcome are separate events.

Compare `journalctl --list-boots`, `journalctl -b -p warning` and `sudo journalctl --since '10 minutes ago'`. Set up persistent storage and flush the journal as described in the previous workshop. Run `logger -t shift-handoff 'dispatch verified'` and look it up with `sudo journalctl -b -t shift-handoff`. Run `sudo journalctl --sync` and reboot your disposable guest. On the new boot, search `sudo journalctl -b -1 -t shift-handoff`. If boot -1 is unavailable, check the configured Storage setting and whether a persistent journal directory exists. Write a fresh marker and repeat after changing the setting.

**Independent ticket.** A manager asks for proof that the failed service ran on the *prior* boot. Supply its unit name, the earlier boot ID, one diagnostic line and its exit status. Explain why an old log line from a different boot could lead the next shift to change a healthy service.

lessons.title: Practice a one-time boot change and restore normal startup
lessons.body:
Use a disposable clone with a working console and a known root password for rescue-mode authentication. On your own clone with a locked root account, an authorized sudo administrator can set a temporary root password before the exercise with `sudo passwd root`.

In the untimed server, run `systemctl get-default`, `systemctl list-units --type=target --state=active` and `cat /proc/cmdline`. The configured default is the goal for a normal startup. The running boot can have reached several targets at once.

## Self-check at a local VM console
Use a disposable AlmaLinux 10 guest with a visible bootloader console and known authorized administrative credentials for rescue mode. Some cloud images lock the root account or hide the early boot menu. Use a suitable console-equipped practice image for this exercise. Keep the graded pair's boot options intact.

At the GRUB menu highlight the current kernel, press `e`, append `systemd.unit=rescue.target` to the kernel command line, and use the on-screen boot key (usually Ctrl+x). Authenticate when prompted. Run `cat /proc/cmdline` and `systemctl is-active rescue.target`. Resume normal service with `systemctl default`. Reboot normally and confirm the one-time kernel argument has disappeared. For a headless server, practice configuring `multi-user.target` as the default with `sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target`. Verify with `systemctl get-default`. Restore the original default when finished.

On an AlmaLinux guest with `grubby`, inspect `sudo grubby --info=DEFAULT`. Practice a reversible persistent change to the default kernel entry: save its path using `kernel=$(sudo grubby --default-kernel)`, and record the path outside the VM. Use an entry whose args contain no existing systemd.show_status setting. Add an informational argument with `sudo grubby --update-kernel="$kernel" --args="systemd.show_status=yes"`, then inspect the entry. After booting that entry, check `/proc/cmdline`. Remove only your added argument with `sudo grubby --update-kernel="$kernel" --remove-args="systemd.show_status=yes"`, reselecting the saved path if you logged in anew. Start and stop guests cleanly with `sudo systemctl reboot` and `sudo systemctl poweroff` in a disposable console exercise.

lessons.title: Repair a failed mount from the guest console
lessons.body:
At power-on the firmware starts the bootloader, which loads a kernel and an initial RAM filesystem. That early environment finds the real root filesystem. The kernel starts systemd, which brings up the configured target and its units. A misspelled data-volume UUID is a useful diagnostic case: the kernel may boot normally while a later mount fails.

## Rehearse recovery on a disposable clone
Use a powered-off snapshot of a VM you administer, with a working hypervisor console and a known root password for rescue login. If the root account is locked on your own clone, an authorized sudo administrator can set a temporary root password there with `sudo passwd root` before the drill. Keep this clone separate from the timed guests. Save a known-good copy with `sudo cp -p /etc/fstab /root/fstab.before-drill`. Run `systemctl get-default` and `findmnt -T /` and record both.

Create /mnt/drill on the clone and add the following line to /etc/fstab in an editor. The label intentionally names a nonexistent practice filesystem. The noauto flag keeps it out of the normal startup transaction.

```text
LABEL=ABSENTDRILL /mnt/drill ext4 noauto 0 0
```

Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and request the mount explicitly with `sudo mount /mnt/drill`. Read the diagnostic and compare the label with `lsblk -f`. The declared identity cannot be resolved. At the guest console reboot and use the preceding lesson's one-boot rescue target. Authenticate, compare the active target and the saved default, and fix only the added line with your editor. You can check your work against /root/fstab.before-drill using diff. Run `systemctl daemon-reload` and `findmnt --verify`. Return to normal service, reboot, and verify the recorded default and root mount. A preexisting warning needs separate interpretation; your practice error should be gone.

**Independent ticket.** Explain at which boot stage your practice definition would matter if it were required automatically. Show how you would distinguish a missing device from a wrong filesystem type, using its signature and an observed error. The exercise leaves ordinary boot available even if you need more time to finish.

lessons.title: Recover root access by interrupting the boot
lessons.body:
A server's root password has been lost and no account with sudo remains. With console access you can stop the boot early, set a new password and let SELinux repair the changed file's label. Practice only on a disposable RHEL 10 guest whose boot menu you can reach and whose disk is not encrypted. Keep the graded pair's boot options intact.

## Reset the password from an early shell
At the GRUB menu highlight the current kernel and press `e`. On the line that starts with `linux`, remove `rhgb quiet` so messages stay visible, then append `rd.break`. Boot with the on-screen key (usually Ctrl+x). At the `switch_root` prompt the installed system is mounted read-only at `/sysroot`.

```sh
mount -o remount,rw /sysroot
chroot /sysroot
passwd root
touch /.autorelabel
exit
exit
```

The first `exit` leaves the chroot and the second resumes startup. The relabel runs once and reboots the guest; let it finish. Log in as root with the new password and confirm with `id` and `getenforce`.

## Why the relabel matters
`passwd` writes a new `/etc/shadow`. The early shell does not load the SELinux policy, so the new file can get the wrong label, and a system with a mislabeled shadow file can reject every login. `/.autorelabel` asks the next normal boot to restore default contexts across the filesystem.

## An alternative entry point
If the early shell lacks `chroot`, edit the `linux` line again: change `ro` to `rw`, remove `rhgb quiet` and append `init=/bin/bash`. The root filesystem is then already writable at `/`. Run `passwd root` and `touch /.autorelabel`, then `exec /sbin/init` to continue startup. Either way the edit applies to this boot only. Confirm afterwards with `cat /proc/cmdline` that neither argument remains.

A GRUB password, Secure Boot policy or an encrypted root volume adds its own prompt before you reach a shell. On the exam, read the task for the machine and the account it names.

lessons.title: Lab • Apply a persistent performance profile
lessons.body:
On the **server**, select the provided TuneD `throughput-performance` profile. The server must report that profile after startup without an interactive command.

Inspect the service state, the installed profiles and the chosen profile independently. If the name is present in the profile list but the active profile differs, determine which command selects it. If the choice vanishes after startup, examine the TuneD service and its current-boot journal. Use the grader's before/after observations to check whether your change survived.

## Reason through a reported result
The profile package exists, but tuned-adm active reports a different policy after reboot. What evidence is missing?

**Check your reasoning.** An installed profile is a choice. Verify which profile TuneD selected, that the service is running at startup, and whether the intended settings verify after boot.

lessons.title: Make a service leave evidence on every boot
lessons.body:
A service can be running now and absent after reboot. It can also be enabled and failing on every start. Use a practice oneshot unit to observe what each state means. On the workshop server save the following in `/etc/systemd/system/workshop-stamp.service`.

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Record workshop startup

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/touch /run/workshop-stamp
RemainAfterExit=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload`, then `sudo systemctl start workshop-stamp`. Compare `systemctl is-active workshop-stamp` with `systemctl is-enabled workshop-stamp`. The first should report active and the second disabled on this new unit. Now enable it with `sudo systemctl enable workshop-stamp`. Verify the marker with `stat /run/workshop-stamp`. Record `cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id`, run `sudo systemctl reboot` and reconnect. Confirm the boot ID changed. Inspect `stat /run/workshop-stamp` and `sudo journalctl -b -u workshop-stamp`. The guest recreated /run at startup, so a marker on the new boot is evidence of a fresh invocation.

Self-check: stop the practice unit and predict both state queries before running them. Start it again and inspect `systemctl cat workshop-stamp` and `journalctl -b -u workshop-stamp`. Distinguish the installed definition, systemd's loaded view and the program's actual outcome. A successful oneshot with RemainAfterExit can legitimately show `active (exited)`.

lessons.title: Choose when a job should run and how to prove it ran
lessons.body:
A storage report is needed once after tonight’s maintenance, a second report is needed every weekday morning, and a third should catch up if the machine was off at its scheduled time. Write the three requirements as promises. The mechanism follows from the promise. An at job leaves the queue after it executes. A cron entry describes matching wall-clock minutes. A systemd calendar timer can trigger a paired service and can catch up on a missed event when Persistent=true.

Read `timedatectl` on the guest. Which time zone is in effect? A schedule for 08:00 on a server set to UTC is a different promise from 08:00 local office time. A correctly formatted date can still be wrong if the clock is drifting. Use `chronyc tracking` and `chronyc sources -v` when chronyd is installed. A selected upstream and a recent useful update are better evidence than a running process alone.

## Work it out before editing
Interpret `15 6 * * 1-5` from left to right as minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. On a normally configured cron host this matches weekdays at 06:15 in its scheduling time zone. A user's crontab has five time fields followed by its command. System crontab entries include a username field. Adding that field to a per-user crontab makes cron try to execute that word as a command.

**Independent ticket.** Put the guest's time zone, intended local time and expected next run in your notes. In the following workshop schedule a timestamp into a practice log. Find evidence at three places: the configured schedule, the scheduler's decision, and the output produced by the job. If the job works in your terminal only, compare the command's path, user, working directory and output redirection.

lessons.title: Choose a scheduler and verify its work
lessons.body:
On a disposable guest with at, cronie and chrony installed, run `sudo systemctl enable --now atd crond chronyd`. Check the guest time zone with `timedatectl`. Schedule a job that records a harmless timestamp. In an untimed guest with `at` and `atd` installed and active, run `echo '/usr/bin/date -Is >> /tmp/workshop-once.log' | at now + 2 minutes`. Use `atq` while waiting. The job leaves the queue after execution; check the actual log. For recurring work in an image with cronie and active crond, use `crontab -e` and add `*/2 * * * * /usr/bin/date -Is >> /tmp/workshop-cron.log`. Confirm with `crontab -l`, wait for a matching minute, and remove only your practice line when finished. Absolute paths help when a scheduler has a smaller environment than your interactive shell.

For a systemd alternative, create `/etc/systemd/system/workshop-log.service` with the first block and `/etc/systemd/system/workshop-log.timer` with the second. The shared base name associates the timer with the service.

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Write workshop journal entry
[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/logger -t workshop-timer tick
```

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Run workshop log job
[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* *:*:00
AccuracySec=1s
Persistent=true
[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```

Reload systemd, `sudo systemctl enable --now workshop-log.timer`, and inspect `systemctl list-timers --all workshop-log.timer`. After a minute read `journalctl -t workshop-timer -b`. Stop future activations and remove startup enablement with `sudo systemctl disable --now workshop-log.timer`. For a time client use `timedatectl`, `chronyc sources -v` and `chronyc tracking`. On a guest with a designated reachable NTP source, add one `server YOUR_NTP_SOURCE iburst` directive with the real address to `/etc/chrony.conf`, restart chronyd and check for a selected source (`^*`). If the time server restarted after the client, a configured source can still show ^? while the client waits for usable measurements. Check the route and the server’s NTP firewall rule on the private interface. Once the source is reachable, use `sudo chronyc online` and `sudo chronyc burst 4/4` to request fresh samples. Compare `chronyc -n sources` with `chronyc tracking` and record the selected address and reference ID. The private exam network supplies no time server. Merely starting chronyd does not prove synchronization.

lessons.title: Lab • Restore a startup service
lessons.body:
On the **server**, the supplied `erudior-maint.service` creates a runtime marker. Start it now and enable it for future boots. Inspect the supplied unit before you change its state.

Use two systemctl queries to verify active and enabled independently. Then inspect `/run/erudior-maint.ready` and the unit's journal. If it is active but disabled, decide what the next reboot would do. If it is enabled but failed, read the first error in the current boot. Leave the supplied unit performing its original job and submit for the reboot check.

## Reason through a reported result
Immediately after enabling a unit it still reports inactive. How can both observations be true?

**Check your reasoning.** Enablement connects the unit to a future startup target. Inspect the live status and use the expected runtime marker to distinguish starting now from enabling for boot.

lessons.title: Build a decision from arguments and exit statuses
lessons.body:
A script is a saved series of shell instructions. Its caller needs to know what to pass in, what output to expect and how failure is reported. Start with an ordinary task: label a shipment as small or bulk. For this exercise enter one to four ASCII digits for a package count between 0 and 9999. Leading zeroes are allowed. Writing down the contract lets you decide what to do with 9, 10, an empty input and the word ten.

Save the following in a fresh file called shipment. Use your editor, then inspect the first line before running it.

```sh
#!/bin/sh
if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]; then
    echo 'give one package count' >&2
    exit 2
fi
case "$1" in
    ''|*[!0-9]*|?????*) echo 'use one to four digits' >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
if [ "$1" -lt 10 ]; then
    echo small
else
    echo bulk
fi
```

The first line selects the interpreter. The shell supplies the number of arguments in `$#` and the first argument in `$1`. The test command inside brackets returns an exit status that if uses to choose a branch. Leave spaces around its words. Run `chmod u+x shipment`. Then run `./shipment 9`, `./shipment 10`, `./shipment 0009`, `./shipment 9999`, `./shipment 10000`, `./shipment ten` and `./shipment`. Inspect `echo $?` directly after each. The invalid cases should write a diagnostic and exit 2. The threshold itself belongs in the upper group.

**Independent ticket.** Change the boundary to 25 and process three separate counts without editing the script again. Try `for count in 24 25 26; do ./shipment "$count"; done`. Explain what varies on each iteration and what stays fixed. In the next workshop you will preserve multiple input filenames, including names with spaces, and capture the output of another command inside the script.

lessons.title: Turn a shell command into a testable tool
lessons.body:
The next shift needs a tool that can report on several files without losing a filename that contains spaces. A script has a contract. Specify its arguments, output, exit status and required permissions before you write it.

In your home directory, save this as `line-report`. The first line selects the interpreter when the file is executed directly. Quotes around `"$@"` preserve the original arguments individually.

```sh
#!/bin/sh
if [ "$#" -eq 0 ]; then
    printf '%s\n' 'supply at least one file' >&2
    exit 2
fi
for file in "$@"; do
    if [ -f "$file" ] && [ -r "$file" ]; then
        lines=$(wc -l < "$file") || exit 1
        printf '%s %s\n' "$lines" "$file"
    else
        printf 'unreadable: %s\n' "$file" >&2
        exit 1
    fi
done
```

Run `chmod 755 line-report`. Create a file containing two newline-terminated lines named `shift notes`. Run `./line-report 'shift notes'` and check for `2 shift notes`. Run `./line-report missing >out.txt 2>err.txt`, immediately check `echo $?`, and inspect both files. An error belongs on standard error so the next program can use standard output as data.

## Try a numeric boundary
Make a second executable that reads its first argument as a number and prints `low` below 5 and `high` otherwise. Use the shell numeric test `[ "$1" -lt 5 ]`, leaving spaces around the bracket tokens. Exercise 0, 4, 5 and 17. Try launching the installed script by its full path as a second user. A script that works only when invoked with `bash scriptname` may have a bad shebang or lack execute permission.

lessons.title: Lab • Deliver an executable classifier
lessons.body:
On the **client**, install `/usr/local/bin/lab-classify` as an executable shell script for an unprivileged user. Given one nonnegative integer, it must print exactly `small` below 10 and `large` for 10 or higher. The command should run directly by absolute path.

Write your own tests first. Include 0, 9, 10 and a larger value you choose. Run them as `learner` and compare the exact standard output. If a root-run test works and a learner test fails, inspect the shebang, directory traversal and file mode. Extra prompts or debug output on stdout change the result.

## Reason through a reported result
Running sh /usr/local/bin/lab-classify 10 prints large; executing the file by its full path as learner returns Permission denied. Which part of the contract failed?

**Check your reasoning.** Calling sh reads the script as input and bypasses the direct-execution check. Inspect execute permission and ancestor traversal, then test the full path as learner.

lessons.title: Trace a file down to the disk that holds it
lessons.body:
A directory is a location in the names you can walk through. A filesystem is the structure that stores names, data and metadata. A mount attaches the root of a filesystem at a directory. A partition is a bounded region of a disk. LVM adds another layer that lets logical volumes draw from a shared pool of storage. The size of a disk, a logical volume and a mounted filesystem can legitimately differ.

## Work backwards from a file
Run `findmnt -T /etc/hosts` on your VM. Read SOURCE, TARGET and FSTYPE. Use `lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS` to follow the mount's source toward a disk. On a machine using LVM it may go through a logical volume and a partition. On a simpler installation the filesystem can occupy a partition directly. Compare `df -hT /` with `du -sh ~/shift-practice` if that directory exists. The first reports capacity of the containing filesystem. The second totals a particular directory tree.

**Read this case.** A guest has a 20 GiB virtual disk. One partition occupies 12 GiB and its volume group has 4 GiB free. A mounted XFS logical volume of 5 GiB is full. If you need 1 GiB more there, allocating a new virtual disk is unnecessary. Check free extents in `vgs`, enlarge the correct logical volume, grow the filesystem, then verify the mount gained capacity. Equality between `lsblk` disk size and `df` space would be the wrong success criterion.

## Identify a new practice disk
On a manual VM record your current `lsblk` tree. Power it off, attach one new, empty 2 GiB virtual disk and boot it. Identify the added device by the before/after inventory, size, mountpoints, children and any filesystem signatures. Run `sudo wipefs --no-act DEVICE` with the newly identified path to inspect signatures without changing it. If you cannot distinguish the data disk from the boot disk, use the new temporary file and loop procedure in the next lesson.

**Independent ticket.** Draw the actual layers serving / on your machine. Circle the layer where unused space would need to exist before you could extend an existing LV. Keep a copy of this inventory for comparison after your storage workshop.

lessons.title: Build and extend a disposable LVM volume
lessons.body:
A department needs a filesystem that can grow without moving its existing data. A partition can hold an LVM physical volume (PV). A volume group (VG) pools capacity. A logical volume (LV) draws space from the pool. Growing the LV and growing the filesystem are distinct operations.

## Self-check using a new file as a practice disk
Use a disposable AlmaLinux 10 guest with loop devices, parted, LVM2 and XFS tools. Run the blocks in the same root shell (`sudo -i`). Use only the newly allocated loop device reported below. Stop if `vgs workshp_vg` already finds a group with that name, or `/mnt/workshp_lv` is already in use. This exercise needs about 1 GiB of free space. The regular-file disk lets you practice without repartitioning a system disk.

```sh
diskfile=$(mktemp /var/tmp/rhcsa-disk.XXXXXX)
truncate -s 1G "$diskfile"
loop=$(losetup --find --show --partscan "$diskfile")
losetup "$loop"
parted -s "$loop" mklabel gpt mkpart primary 1MiB 100%
partprobe "$loop"
udevadm settle
part="$loop"p1
lsblk -o PATH,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE "$loop"
```

Confirm the partition path shown by `lsblk` equals `$part`. If the LVM devices file is in use and the partition is not visible to LVM, add only the practice partition with `lvmdevices --adddev "$part"`. An image filtering loop devices may require an attached unused training disk instead. Do not substitute the boot disk.

```sh
pvcreate "$part"
vgcreate workshp_vg "$part"
lvcreate -L 400M -n reports workshp_vg
mkfs.xfs /dev/workshp_vg/reports
mkdir /mnt/workshp_lv
mount /dev/workshp_vg/reports /mnt/workshp_lv
printf 'keep me\n' > /mnt/workshp_lv/proof
df -hT /mnt/workshp_lv
lvextend -L +128M -r /dev/workshp_vg/reports
cat /mnt/workshp_lv/proof
df -hT /mnt/workshp_lv
lvs
```

Expect more space and unchanged proof text. `-r` requests a matching filesystem resize. Use `pvs`, `vgs` and `lvs` to find which layer lacks space if growth fails. A loop mapping lasts only for this exercise. Practice mounting by UUID across reboot on an attached practice disk in the next module.

## Clean up the disk you created
After confirming `losetup "$loop"` still shows your temporary file and `findmnt /mnt/workshp_lv` identifies your practice LV, unmount it. Remove the practice LV, then the VG, then its PV label using `lvremove /dev/workshp_vg/reports`, `vgremove workshp_vg` and `pvremove "$part"`. If you added the partition to the LVM devices file, remove its entry if still present. Delete partition 1 on that loop disk with `parted -s "$loop" rm 1`, detach with `losetup -d "$loop"`, then remove your temporary file and empty mount directory. Check `lvs` and `losetup -j "$diskfile"` to confirm retirement.

lessons.title: Activate swap and make it return at startup
lessons.body:
Swap supplies extra backing space for idle memory pages. An allocated file, a swap signature, activation now and a boot-time entry are four distinct states. On the untimed server inspect `free -h`, `swapon --show --bytes`, `df -h /var/lib` and `findmnt -T /var/lib`. Use the following on the workshop guest's local XFS or ext4 filesystem. Choose a fresh path and ensure at least 70 MiB is free.

```sh
sudo sh -c 'set -C; umask 077; dd if=/dev/zero bs=1M count=65 status=none > /var/lib/workshop.swap'
```

If creation failed or the path already existed, stop and choose a new path. Inspect the resulting regular file and mode with `sudo stat /var/lib/workshop.swap`. Initialize your new file with `sudo mkswap /var/lib/workshop.swap` and activate it with `sudo swapon /var/lib/workshop.swap`. Verify the name and size with `swapon --show --bytes`. Allocating real blocks avoids sparse-file activation errors.

Edit `/etc/fstab` and add one line `/var/lib/workshop.swap none swap defaults 0 0` after confirming that path has no existing entry. Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and `sudo findmnt --verify`. Reboot the untimed guest and run `swapon --show` again. A clean configuration file alone cannot prove that the kernel activated the space.

## Swap on a new partition or logical volume
Tasks often ask for swap on new block storage instead of a file. On a disposable guest with an attached practice disk, create a partition with `parted` (type it `linux-swap` with `mkpart swap linux-swap 1MiB 513MiB`) or a new LV with `lvcreate -L 512M -n swap2 VG`. Leave existing partitions and volumes untouched. Run `mkswap` on the new device and note the UUID it prints. Add a line such as `UUID=actual-uuid none swap defaults 0 0`, then run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and `sudo swapon -a`. Confirm the new device in `swapon --show` before and after a reboot. A swap device has no mountpoint, so its fstab line uses `none` and the type `swap`.

lessons.title: Add capacity without disturbing existing data
lessons.body:
A branch can attach a second disk but cannot take the archive offline. A volume group can combine physical volumes so an existing logical volume can grow. The existing filesystem keeps its identity. Your job is to prove both that the data survived and that the new capacity reached the application.

On a disposable manual VM, attach two fresh virtual disks of 2 GiB each. Take an inventory before and after, then work only on these confirmed empty disks. Use the GPT and LVM workshop procedure on the first disk to make a VG named branchtest and a 512 MiB LV called inbox. Give it ext4 with `mkfs.ext4`, mount it at /mnt/branchtest and create a file containing a handoff note. Record its checksum and `df -B1 /mnt/branchtest`. Leave existing system partitions and VGs alone.

Use `sudo parted DEVICE print` to identify the second disposable disk, replacing DEVICE with its verified path. A blank disk can report an unrecognized disk label. Following the partitioning procedure in the LVM workshop, create a GPT with one partition, settle device discovery and inspect the new partition path. In the commands below set `newpart` to that actual partition. On a host using the LVM devices file, add that practice partition to the devices file if necessary.

```sh
sudo pvcreate "$newpart"
sudo vgextend branchtest "$newpart"
sudo pvs -o pv_name,vg_name,pv_free
sudo lvextend -L +256M /dev/branchtest/inbox "$newpart"
sudo resize2fs /dev/branchtest/inbox
df -hT /mnt/branchtest
```

The LV grows first. resize2fs expands the mounted ext4 filesystem to use the larger device. An XFS filesystem instead grows online through its mountpoint with xfs_growfs. The earlier workshop used lvextend -r to request both operations together. Read the note again and compare its checksum. A larger LV with an unchanged filesystem size is unfinished work.

**Independent ticket.** Report the new PV, the VG's remaining free space, the larger filesystem and the matching checksum. Use the mount-by-UUID exercise to add persistence on your clone. For cleanup, remove any practice fstab entry, reload systemd, unmount your test filesystem, and retire the LV, VG and both PV labels only after identifying each against your recorded inventory. Remove your test disks in the hypervisor only when the clone no longer depends on them.

lessons.title: Lab • Add persistent swap capacity
lessons.body:
On the **server**, add an active swap file at `/var/lib/erudior.swap` with at least 64 MiB of file allocation and make it activate automatically at boot. Leave existing swap and filesystem entries intact. Use a 65 MiB file in this exercise. The kernel reserves a header, so swapon reports slightly less usable space than the file length.

Use `swapon --show --bytes` to confirm the path and usable size. Check that the regular file is private to root, its entry appears once in `/etc/fstab`, and the file is fully allocated. If the grader sees the file now but loses it after boot, inspect the boot-time configuration and swap unit journal.

## Reason through a reported result
The swap file is 65 MiB and was present after reboot, yet swapon --show lists only the original device. Has the new swap helped?

**Check your reasoning.** Its file survived, but the kernel has not activated it. Check the exact fstab path and swap type, verify configuration and repeat the activation check.

lessons.title: Explain why a file disappears under a mount
lessons.body:
A colleague remembers putting handoff.txt in /mnt/dispatch. You see an empty directory at that location. Before deciding anyone deleted data, ask which filesystem currently supplies the path. A mount can cover files in an existing directory. Unmounting exposes them again.

On a disposable guest pick a fresh directory under your home with `work=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/mount-practice.XXXXXX")`. Save the original marker with `printf 'underneath\n' > "$work/handoff.txt"`. Record `findmnt -T "$work"`. Mount a small temporary memory filesystem with `sudo mount -t tmpfs -o size=8m tmpfs "$work"` and inspect `findmnt -T "$work"` and `ls -la "$work"` again. The first marker seems to have vanished. Add a different marker with `echo visible | sudo tee "$work/live.txt"`. Before unmounting, predict which marker will remain.

From outside the mounted directory, run `sudo umount "$work"`, then `ls -la "$work"` and `cat "$work/handoff.txt"`. This new listing comes from the original filesystem. The temporary filesystem is gone. Remove your original marker and the empty temporary directory when finished. If a real unmount says busy, first check whether a shell is using the mount as its working directory.

**Independent ticket.** A backup job wrote 200 MiB into a directory before the data disk mounted. After the mount, the files disappear and space on the root filesystem stays low. Draw the two storage locations. State which source you would verify before moving any data. In the next workshop, use a marker, a UUID and a reboot to prove which filesystem serves a path.

lessons.title: Mount the right filesystem and prove what is serving a path
lessons.body:
On the server inspect `lsblk -f`, `findmnt -T /` and `sudo blkid`. Device names can change after hardware changes. A filesystem UUID or unique label identifies the intended filesystem across boots. A mounted filesystem also hides whatever was in the mount directory underneath it.

## Self-check with disposable filesystems
Use the new-file and loop procedure in **Build and extend a disposable LVM volume** on a disposable guest, with a fresh backing file for each filesystem. For each new empty partition, choose **one** formatter: `mkfs.ext4 -L TRAINEXT "$part"`, `mkfs.xfs -L TRAINXFS "$part"`, or `mkfs.vfat -n TRAINVF "$part"`. VFAT needs dosfstools. Never reformat a partition whose data you intend to keep. Create an empty practice mountpoint, mount the partition, write and read a marker, and use `findmnt -T /path/to/marker` to record the source and type. Unmount, verify the marker disappears, remount and verify it returns. VFAT generally expresses ownership and masks through mount options.

For a boot test, use a persistent, attached practice disk. Mount its filesystem by UUID or by LABEL at a new path. For example, with an ext4 volume add a single `UUID=actual-uuid /mnt/reports ext4 defaults 0 2` line to `/etc/fstab`, using the real identifier from `blkid`. Create the mountpoint, unmount any manual mount, reload systemd, run `sudo findmnt --verify` and `sudo mount /mnt/reports`. Verify the source and marker after a reboot. Remove the entry before retiring the disk.

## Self-check the network path
In the untimed client, mount the supplied server export once at a separate empty location. Run `sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs-check`, `sudo mount -t nfs -o ro 192.168.77.10:/srv/projects /mnt/nfs-check` and inspect the marker with `findmnt -T /mnt/nfs-check/erudior-lab.txt`.
